extend.why: Lead 4 is the Da Nang Priority Infrastructure Investment Project, P086508, credit IDA-44020, in the same city and at the same coordinates as the case written for lead 11, and the two credits are one continuing episode. The later project took the earlier one's unfinished works and its remaining land acquisition and resettlement as its own Component 5, named "Transferred Activities from Da Nang Priority Infrastructure Investment Project", at an actual cost of US$26.94 million; the earlier project's completion report says its resettlement was completed satisfactorily except for the acquisitions and resettlements transferred to the later project. Two cards at one point for one episode would be wrong, so the earlier credit is added to the existing card rather than mapped again. The earlier credit also has no documented failure of its own.

fields_add.community: The earlier credit paid for a southern ring road, a southern link road, drainage and sanitation works and upgrading in 13 low income areas. Its completion report of 19 December 2013 says the project acquired around 189.1 hectares of land and affected 3,518 households, of which 1,670 lost agricultural land. On how many were resettled the two Bank documents give different numbers. The completion report says, in its safeguards section and again in the borrower's section, that of the 3,518 households 936 "were only partially affected and had to be resettled", and that the number of resettled households rose by 12 per cent against the 711 originally planned. The Independent Evaluation Group's review of 23 October 2014 repeats the 936 in its own safeguards section and, in its list of the project's outputs, states that "796 households were resettled, compared to 711 originally planned". Both figures are printed here and neither document reconciles them. The completion report gives two reasons for the increase over plan: some households split their plots, two families living on one plot dividing it in two, and some households moved voluntarily to better resettlement areas closer to the Southern Link Road route. Three resettlement areas were built on 18.3 hectares in total, at Thanh Khe Tay, Hoa Minh and Hoa Quy. The Bank's section of the report says the project provided 613 lots and 198 apartments for relocated households and a school with 20 rooms for children of affected households; the borrower's section gives 1,098 lots and 110 apartments at the sites, of which 287 lots and 56 apartments were funded by this project and 811 lots and 54 apartments by the city. The report says most compensation was completed as planned, that compensation and resettlement for the southern ring road was finished by June 2013 except for the activities transferred to the later project, that all relocated households were allocated land plots at a resettlement site, that Da Nang used sites inside people's own neighbourhoods to meet their wish to stay nearby, and that the grievance system worked well. The independent resettlement monitoring consultant is quoted in the Group's review as certifying that "almost all Project affected people have been able to restore their lost assets and livelihoods." The physical cultural resources policy was triggered by the relocation of some graves and by two temples and four houses of worship in the project area; the report says consultation at appraisal found the affected people willing to relocate if compensated and given alternative sites, and that there were no adverse impacts at closure. Delays in negotiating relocation, land acquisition and resettlement are recorded in both documents as holding up construction. No individual household or community is named.
fields_add.outcome: The earlier credit's completion report of 19 December 2013 rates its outcome Moderately Satisfactory, and the Independent Evaluation Group's review of 23 October 2014 keeps that rating. The Group records that works worth an estimated US$16.6 million, 25 per cent of the appraisal estimate, were moved to the later project, records shortcomings in the handling of land acquisition and relocation that delayed construction, and prints among the project's lessons that "relocation and resettlement should be minimized".
fields_add.displaced_note: For the earlier credit the Bank's documents give two counts of households resettled. Its completion report says 936 of 3,518 affected households had to be resettled and that the number rose 12 per cent against the 711 planned. The Independent Evaluation Group's review says 936 in its safeguards section and 796 in its list of outputs. 1,670 households lost agricultural land. ICIJ puts displacement for the earlier project at 13,788 and lists it in its confirmed-displacement table; no figure of 13,788 appears in these documents and they do not explain the gap.

extend.why: Lead 8 is the same loan as this case: the Uganda Transport Sector Development Project, P092837, whose cancellation the card already records. The existing card covers the Kamwenge-Fort Portal road and rests on the Inspection Panel's investigation. The project's own completion report adds firmer loan figures, its own compensation figures for that road, the Bank's verdict on the safeguards category, and compensation shortfalls on two other corridors paid for by the same credits. Those two corridors are a different place and are added as a fact about the credits, not as part of this episode.

lenders_add.name: World Bank (IDA), full credit detail
lenders_add.role: Credit IDA-46790, SDR 120 million (US$190 million equivalent), approved 10 December 2009 and effective 15 July 2010; additional credit IDA-49490, SDR 47.4 million (US$75 million equivalent), approved by the Board in 2010 and signed later; and grant TF-11094 of GBP 6.05 million (US$8.0 million equivalent) from the United Kingdom's Department for International Development, for the Transport Sector Development Project (P092837). The revised commitment was SDR 106.96 million. The Bank suspended disbursements on 22 October 2015 for the borrower's failure to implement the project in line with environmental and social standards, and cancelled the project on 21 December 2015 with the Kamwenge-Fort Portal road 49 per cent complete; the government continued the road with its own funds. fields_add.community: The completion report gives its own compensation figures for this road: 2,246 of 2,844 identified people had been compensated, 79 per cent, rising to 94 per cent by 27 March 2017. It says the original estimate of 2,430 people was based on sampling rather than a full census, and that a later sweep by surveyors and valuation experts added another 414 people eligible for compensation. These are a different count from the Inspection Panel's 2,455 people owed resettlement pay with 209 claims still outstanding in mid-2016; the two sources count at different dates and neither document reconciles them. The report says the significant social concerns the communities raised, including sexual violence against children by road workers, increased child labour and school dropouts, more accidents on the road and at the stone quarry, a rise in crime, poor compensation practices and an unclear redress mechanism, 'were not responded to adequately in a timely manner'. The same credits also paid for two roads in northern Uganda, which are not part of this episode, and the completion report gives compensation shortfalls on both. On the Gulu-Atiak road, 1,884 of 2,027 affected people were compensated, 93 per cent, with ten of the unpaid claims in court and the rest awaiting reassessment. On the Vurra-Oraba road, 3,276 of 3,935 were compensated, 83 per cent; the report says the shortfall arose because extra affected people were identified after compensation was supposed to have been concluded and no money had been budgeted for land acquisition that year, and records in a footnote 'over 200 complaints of non-payment due to bounced payments and missing documentation'.
fields_add.conditions: The 2011 environmental and social impact assessment for the Kamwenge-Fort Portal road proposed category A; during preparation of the additional financing this was downgraded to category B. The Bank's completion report says that given the complex and systemic social issues that emerged during implementation and the fact that the road runs through a national park, 'this change in the safeguard category was an error of judgment'. A 13.3 km section of the road crosses Kibale National Park, where the design had originally kept the road unwidened to avoid taking land and destroying tree canopies, partly to reduce road kills of primates crossing at road level. On 22 December 2014 the Uganda Wildlife Authority approved the wider cross-section through the park, an option the impact assessment had rejected, on condition that only a limited number of trees be removed and additional speed humps installed.
fields_add.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 12,882 for this project. The Bank's completion report counts people identified for compensation rather than people relocated: 2,027 on Gulu-Atiak, 3,935 on Vurra-Oraba and 2,844 on Kamwenge-Fort Portal. The documents do not explain how ICIJ's figure was arrived at.

extend.why: Lead 27, Madagascar's Integrated Growth Poles project (P083351), is the World Bank operation the existing card already names through MIGA's guarantee. Its completion report puts an IDA credit behind the resettlement plans for the QMM mine and the Ehoala port and records the land-price disputes and roadblocks. This adds the loan and those findings rather than making a second case at the same place.

lenders_add.name: World Bank (IDA), Integrated Growth Poles Project
lenders_add.role: The Integrated Growth Poles Project (P083351) was approved on 12 July 2005, became effective on 28 September 2005 and closed on 31 December 2014 against an original closing date of 31 December 2010. It was financed by credits IDA-41010 and IDA-43990, with an original commitment of SDR 85.90 million revised to SDR 107.56 million and SDR 107.31 million disbursed; the additional credit of SDR 25 million (US$40 million) was approved by the Bank's board in April 2008 and the financing agreement signed on 8 May 2008. The project covered Antananarivo-Antsirabe, Nosy Be and Taolagnaro (Fort Dauphin). Its Fort Dauphin component built a new public port on the Ehoala peninsula under a public-private partnership with Rio Tinto and part-rehabilitated the existing port. The Bank's completion report lists, among the component's safeguards activities, 'implementation of RAPs for the QMM's mining facility and Ehoala Port' and water supply and sanitation schemes for project-affected people. Because the Bank financed Ehoala Port as an associated investment supporting Rio Tinto's mining, Rio Tinto also had to comply with Bank safeguard policies. The project was environmental category A and an independent expert advisory panel monitored safeguards compliance during preparation and implementation (World Bank Implementation Completion and Results Report, 15 June 2015).

fields_add.community: The Bank's completion report says QMM's mining investment 'also created significant safeguards challenges in the mining communes', that the income and livelihood restoration programme QMM ran for residents of the mining communes 'was marked by recurring disputes over the prices the company paid to buy their land and the employment policy at its mining facility', and that this prompted local residents at various times to roadblock QMM construction sites and facilities, 'with the most recent flare up in early 2013 when they blocked the mine compound entrance, trapping more than 200 staff inside'. It says the grievance mechanisms the Bank set up during the project and QMM's social programmes helped manage the disputes and prevent violent escalation, but that 'some tensions linger' among residents 'who still feel they were unfairly compensated'. A footnote records that an independent audit of the project's resettlement action plan was launched in 2014 to examine compliance with paragraph 24 of OP 4.12 and paragraph 16 of BP 4.12, and refers to 'PAPs that have yet to obtain compensation at agreed levels following the RAP Audit'. A table in the report's annex, sourced to Rio Tinto's own 2009 information report, lists 'support to the populations affected by the resettlement scheme' through monetary compensation, restitution in kind, house rehabilitation and support measures, naming the resettled population, affected people at Ilafitsinana and villagers from Lohalovoka and Ambinanibe; the same table lists compensation to fishermen and to the people of Ambinanibe, Lohalovoka and Ilafitsinana. The report also records an acute bout of consumer price inflation during construction of the mine and the port, declining employment after the construction period, and an increased risk of HIV/AIDS.
fields_add.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 8,911 displaced for Madagascar's Integrated Growth Poles project, drawn from World Bank documents and current to 31 December 2014. The Bank's completion report for that project names the resettlement plans and the villages involved but gives no count of households or people relocated, and the figures in its annex come from Rio Tinto's own report rather than from the Bank. The documents do not explain how ICIJ's figure was arrived at.

extend.why: Lead 20, the Ethiopia Irrigation and Drainage Project (P092353), is the same episode as this existing case: the same credit, the same two irrigation schemes and the Ribb dam, the same years and the same completion report. It was drafted as a new case and is instead an extend. It adds the credit numbers, the Bank's finding that the project was out of compliance with OP 4.12, and the first independent field study found on this resettlement, which gives the number of households actually relocated and where they went. It also corrects the card's displacement figure, which at present is ICIJ's estimate.

lenders_add.name: World Bank (IDA), full credit detail
lenders_add.role: Credits IDA-43330 and IDA-49760 for the Ethiopia Irrigation and Drainage Project, also called the Ethiopian Nile Irrigation and Drainage Project (P092353). sources_add.title: Effects of Resettlement Schemes on the Livelihood of Project Affected Households: The Case of Ribb Irrigation Dam, Amhara Regional State, Ethiopia (master's thesis, College of Development Studies)

fields_add.conditions: Seven resettlement action plans were approved by the Bank, three for Megech-Seraba, one for Ribb and three for the Ribb dam, with compensation and livelihood restoration costed at US$21.7 million, of which the government funded US$11.17 million. The Bank's policy required compensation before works began. At the final restructuring in October 2017 the financing plan was changed so that credit money could pay US$9.68 million in cash compensation to 6,618 affected people and livelihood restoration payments to 1,486 of them, after the credit had closed.
fields_add.community: A 2020 master's thesis at Addis Ababa University by Teketel Adefres is the first independent field study found on this resettlement. Citing the Ethiopian Ministry of Water, Irrigation and Energy's livelihood relocation report of May 2018, it gives 1,486 households on the final net list of affected households, of whom 227 lost all their farmland and housing and were relocated to the towns of Ebinat and Debre Tabor, 38 households to Ebinat and 189 to Debre Tabor, where they were given urban plots for houses and working areas for licensed groups. The affected kebeles it names, from the same ministry report, are Medeb Gubda, Jara Shekera and Ayva Niva in Farta woreda and Ziha and Amisteya in Ibinat woreda. Adefres surveyed 115 of those 227 relocated households with a questionnaire. Of the 115 who answered, he reports that 6.96 per cent had access to all of the basic services he measured together, which he lists as clean energy, clean water supply, sanitation, road access, school, finance, market access and due compensation; that 8.7 per cent had received income-generating activities; and that 33.0 per cent had market access. He concludes that almost all of the resettled households are leading unsustainable livelihoods and that women are excluded from livelihood opportunities. These are his own survey findings, from one master's thesis, not an established record.
fields_add.outcome: The Bank's completion report says social safeguards performance was unsatisfactory 'primarily due to protracted delays in making compensation payments and supporting livelihood restoration for the PAPs in the Ribb reservoir and dam construction site', that the delays caused 'increasing frustration on the part of the affected communities and rising tension in the project areas', and that 'throughout much of the project implementation period, the project was not in compliance with OP 4.12 and posed high social risk. It was only after credit closure that the project could be brought into compliance through the use of the Credit to cover the costs.' Of the 4,000 hectares targeted at Megech-Seraba only 1,000 hectares were ready for use, the Bank's economic analysis at closing found the project not economically viable, and Bank management refused a further extension.
fields_add.confidence_note: The unpaid compensation, the breach of the Bank's own resettlement policy and the tension in the project areas are stated in the World Bank's own completion report and repeated in the Independent Evaluation Group's review, which are the lender reporting on its own project. The count of 227 relocated households, the towns they were moved to and the living conditions afterwards come from one independent source, a 2020 Addis Ababa University master's thesis, which cites an Ethiopian ministry relocation report of 2018 for the counts and reports its own survey of 115 of the 227 households for the conditions.
